# Joining and Reshaping {#sec-joins} A join can fail in two ways, and neither raises an error. First, it can drop rows. This happens when a key present on one side is absent on the other. The analysis then proceeds on a smaller, and possibly different, cohort than the one the methods section describes. Second, it can multiply rows. This happens when a key that should be unique is not. A patient then contributes several times to an estimate that assumed one contribution. The first failure shrinks the denominator, and the second corrupts the standard errors. In both cases the data frame looks like the one you wanted. Simple arithmetic catches both. We state how many rows the result should have, and check that against how many it does. ::: {.bookepigraph} ```{=latex} \begin{flushright}\small ``` *Only connect.* [E. M. Forster]{.smallcaps}, *Howards End* (1910) ```{=latex} \end{flushright} ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Where this chapter sits: joining and reshaping are part of the Wrangle stage, which turns raw tables into the derived analytic dataset.](15-joins_files/figure-pdf/fig-joins-pipeline-1.pdf){#fig-joins-pipeline fig-align='center' fig-alt='Diagram of the analysis pipeline: six stages in order (Plan, Acquire, Wrangle, Analyze, Report, Share) above two bands that run under every stage (Version control and Environment). Highlighted for this chapter: Wrangle.' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note title='In this chapter'} **Reading time.** About 25 minutes. **You'll need.** @sec-wrangling for the single-table verbs and `pivot_longer()`/`pivot_wider()`, and @sec-types for column types. The code uses: ```r library(dplyr) library(tidyr) library(tidyverse) library(janitor) ``` **You'll be able to.** - Choose the join that answers a stated question and predict its row count before you run it. - Declare the expected relationship and the unmatched behavior, so that the join refuses data that violate them. - Audit keys for uniqueness, type, and coverage with `count()` and `anti_join()` before joining. - Reshape and stack sources with different conventions so that a later join cannot multiply rows. **Outline.** - [Choosing a join](#sec-joins-choosing) - [Cardinality: when a join multiplies rows](#sec-joins-cardinality) - [Keys and referential integrity](#sec-joins-keys) - [Reshaping and stacking sources](#sec-joins-reshaping) - [Worked example: a multi-source patient cohort](#sec-joins-worked) ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Skip ahead?'} If these answers come quickly, skip to the next chapter. The answers are in @sec-quiz-answers-15. 1. What is the difference in row count between `inner_join()` and `left_join()` when the right table is missing some keys that appear in the left table? 2. What does `anti_join()` return, and in a biomedical cleanup workflow, what question does it answer? 3. Given two tables each with a `patient_id` column and a many-to-one relationship (many rows per patient in table A, one row per patient in table B), how do you attach the table-B row to every table-A row? ::: ## Choosing a join {#sec-joins-choosing} Almost every biostatistical project joins tables: demographics to outcomes, labs to medications, clinical data to imaging indices. The operation is one function call. The difficulty lies in the question the join is meant to answer, and in what the keys actually contain. The generic tour of the two-table verbs is in R for Data Science [@wickham2023r4ds, ch. 19]. In this chapter we keep to the judgments that a clinical dataset requires. ### The `_join` family `dplyr`'s two-table verbs: | Function | Returns | |----------------|----------------------------------------------------| | `inner_join` | Rows with a match in both | | `left_join` | All rows from `x`, NA in `y` columns where no match | | `right_join` | All rows from `y`, NA in `x` columns where no match | | `full_join` | All rows from both, NA in non-matching columns | | `semi_join` | Rows of `x` with a match in `y` (no `y` cols) | | `anti_join` | Rows of `x` with no match in `y` | `semi_join` and `anti_join` are filtering joins. They filter `x` based on `y` without adding `y`'s columns. The other four are mutating joins, which add columns.[^pandas] The choice among the mutating joins comes down to two questions, shown in @fig-join-choice. Do you want to keep rows that fail to match? If so, from which side? [^pandas]: In `pandas`, the four mutating joins are one call, `x.merge(y, on="id", how=...)` with `how` set to `"inner"`, `"left"`, `"right"`, or `"outer"`. The filtering joins have no `merge` equivalent and are written with `isin()`, for example `x[~x["id"].isin(y["id"])]` for an anti-join. ```{mermaid} %%| echo: false %%| label: fig-join-choice %%| fig-alt: "Decision flowchart for choosing a join. The first %%| question asks whether to keep rows with no match: no gives %%| inner_join. Yes leads to a second question asking which side %%| the unmatched rows come from: left x gives left_join, right y %%| gives right_join, and both gives full_join." %%| fig-cap: "Choosing a join. The first question is whether unmatched %%| rows should survive; the second is from which table. The %%| filtering joins (semi, anti) answer a different question again: %%| keep or drop rows of x by their presence in y, adding no columns." flowchart TD Q1{"Keep rows with
no match?"} Q1 -->|"No"| INNER["inner_join"] Q1 -->|"Yes"| Q2{"Unmatched from
which side?"} Q2 -->|"Left x"| LEFT["left_join"] Q2 -->|"Right y"| RIGHT["right_join"] Q2 -->|"Both"| FULL["full_join"] ``` The question determines the join: | Question | Join | |---|---| | Patients with both demographics and an outcome | `inner_join` | | All patients, with their outcomes if any | `left_join`, demographics on the left | | Patients with demographics but no outcome | `anti_join` | | All patients from both files, even those in only one | `full_join` | ### Row counts on a toy example The `dplyr` package ships two toy tables, `band_members` and `band_instruments`, that make the row-count differences concrete. Before you run the chunk, predict how many rows each join returns. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(dplyr) band_members #> # A tibble: 3 x 2 #> name band #> #> 1 Mick Stones #> 2 John Beatles #> 3 Paul Beatles band_instruments #> # A tibble: 3 x 2 #> name plays #> #> 1 John guitar #> 2 Paul bass #> 3 Keith guitar inner_join(band_members, band_instruments, by = "name") # John, Paul #> # A tibble: 2 x 3 #> name band plays #> #> 1 John Beatles guitar #> 2 Paul Beatles bass left_join(band_members, band_instruments, by = "name") # + Mick (NA) #> # A tibble: 3 x 3 #> name band plays #> #> 1 Mick Stones #> 2 John Beatles guitar #> 3 Paul Beatles bass full_join(band_members, band_instruments, by = "name") # + Keith (NA) #> # A tibble: 4 x 3 #> name band plays #> #> 1 Mick Stones #> 2 John Beatles guitar #> 3 Paul Beatles bass #> 4 Keith guitar anti_join(band_members, band_instruments, by = "name") # Mick only #> # A tibble: 1 x 2 #> name band #> #> 1 Mick Stones ``` ::: ::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'} Write your predictions down as assertions. The chunk prints nothing when every prediction holds, and stops at the first one that does not. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} stopifnot( nrow(inner_join(band_members, band_instruments, by = "name")) == 2, nrow(left_join(band_members, band_instruments, by = "name")) == nrow(band_members), nrow(full_join(band_members, band_instruments, by = "name")) == 4, nrow(anti_join(band_members, band_instruments, by = "name")) == 1 ) ``` ::: ::: ### Exercises 1. Use each of `inner_join`, `left_join`, `full_join`, and `anti_join` with the built-in `dplyr::band_members` and `dplyr::band_instruments` to produce four different tibbles. Write one sentence per result. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} inner_join(band_members, band_instruments, by = "name") #> # A tibble: 2 x 3 #> name band plays #> #> 1 John Beatles guitar #> 2 Paul Beatles bass left_join(band_members, band_instruments, by = "name") #> # A tibble: 3 x 3 #> name band plays #> #> 1 Mick Stones #> 2 John Beatles guitar #> 3 Paul Beatles bass full_join(band_members, band_instruments, by = "name") #> # A tibble: 4 x 3 #> name band plays #> #> 1 Mick Stones #> 2 John Beatles guitar #> 3 Paul Beatles bass #> 4 Keith guitar anti_join(band_members, band_instruments, by = "name") #> # A tibble: 1 x 2 #> name band #> #> 1 Mick Stones ``` ::: `inner_join` keeps only John and Paul, who appear in both. `left_join` keeps all three band members, giving Mick an `NA` instrument. `full_join` keeps Keith as well, giving him an `NA` band. `anti_join` returns Mick alone, the band member with no instrument row, and adds no columns. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** A collaborator asks for 'the patients in the demographics file who have no outcome record'. Which join answers this, and how many columns of the outcome table does the result carry? **Answer.** `anti_join(demographics, outcomes, by = "patient_id")`. It is a filtering join, so it carries none of the outcome table's columns. It returns rows of `demographics` only. A `left_join` followed by `filter(is.na(outcome))` gives the same patients, but with two drawbacks. It adds columns you then have to drop. It also misreads a patient whose outcome record exists with a missing value as a patient with no record. ::: ## Cardinality: when a join multiplies rows {#sec-joins-cardinality} ### Many-to-many joins A many-to-many join occurs when both tables have duplicate keys. Each row in the left can match several rows in the right, and the reverse. The result is the product of the matches for each key. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(dplyr) a <- tibble(id = c(1, 1, 2), x = c("a", "b", "c")) b <- tibble(id = c(1, 1, 2), y = c("p", "q", "r")) # Five rows, not three: each id-1 in a joins each id-1 in b, giving # four, plus the single id-2 match. dplyr warns because this is # usually a key error rather than an intention. inner_join(a, b, by = "id") #> Warning in inner_join(a, b, by = "id"): Detected an unexpected many-to-many relationship between `x` and `y`. #> i Row 1 of `x` matches multiple rows in `y`. #> i Row 1 of `y` matches multiple rows in `x`. #> i If a many-to-many relationship is expected, set `relationship = #> "many-to-many"` to silence this warning. #> # A tibble: 5 x 3 #> id x y #> #> 1 1 a p #> 2 1 a q #> 3 1 b p #> 4 1 b q #> 5 2 c r ``` ::: `dplyr` 1.1.0 and later warns by default. Take the warning seriously. On a key that should be unique, it means rows have multiplied. Do not silence it. Instead, declare the relationship you expect: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # explicit; no warning, even with duplicates inner_join(a, b, by = "id", relationship = "many-to-many") #> # A tibble: 5 x 3 #> id x y #> #> 1 1 a p #> 2 1 a q #> 3 1 b p #> 4 1 b q #> 5 2 c r # errors if duplicates exist on either side inner_join(a, b, by = "id", relationship = "one-to-one") #> Error in `inner_join()`: #> ! Each row in `x` must match at most 1 row in `y`. #> i Row 1 of `x` matches multiple rows in `y`. ``` ::: ### Declaring the relationship The common case is many-to-one: several visits per patient, and one demographics row per patient. The rest of the chapter uses the three small tables below. P004 appears in `visits` but not in `demographics`. The audits in @sec-joins-keys are designed to catch this kind of gap. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} demographics <- tibble( patient_id = c("P001", "P002", "P003"), age = c(64, 71, 52), sex = c("F", "M", "F") ) visits <- tibble( visit_id = sprintf("V%02d", 1:6), patient_id = c("P001", "P001", "P002", "P002", "P003", "P004"), sbp = c(148, 141, 155, 149, 132, 139) ) labs <- tibble( visit_id = c("V01", "V01", "V02", "V03"), test_code = c("HGB", "CRE", "HGB", "HGB"), value = c(13.1, 0.9, 13.4, 11.8) ) demographics #> # A tibble: 3 x 3 #> patient_id age sex #> #> 1 P001 64 F #> 2 P002 71 M #> 3 P003 52 F visits #> # A tibble: 6 x 3 #> visit_id patient_id sbp #> #> 1 V01 P001 148 #> 2 V02 P001 141 #> 3 V03 P002 155 #> 4 V04 P002 149 #> 5 V05 P003 132 #> 6 V06 P004 139 labs #> # A tibble: 4 x 3 #> visit_id test_code value #> #> 1 V01 HGB 13.1 #> 2 V01 CRE 0.9 #> 3 V02 HGB 13.4 #> 4 V03 HGB 11.8 ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} visits |> left_join(demographics, by = "patient_id", relationship = "many-to-one") #> # A tibble: 6 x 5 #> visit_id patient_id sbp age sex #> #> 1 V01 P001 148 64 F #> 2 V02 P001 141 64 F #> 3 V03 P002 155 71 M #> 4 V04 P002 149 71 M #> 5 V05 P003 132 52 F #> 6 V06 P004 139 NA # errors if a patient_id appears more than once in demographics ``` ::: The assertion catches the data-quality bug at the join site, where it is easiest to debug. Without it, the bug would appear three scripts later as a standard error that is too small. ::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'} **A one-to-many join multiplies rows without a warning.** `dplyr` warns only when keys repeat on *both* sides. Suppose each visit key is unique, and a patient appears twice in `demographics` (a re-consent appended rather than replaced). Then `left_join(visits, demographics)` quietly returns an extra row for every visit of that patient. Only `relationship = "many-to-one"` turns this into an error. ::: ### Exercises 2. Construct a scenario where an unintended many-to-many join duplicates rows. Write an assertion that catches the duplication before downstream analysis. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # demographics has a duplicated patient, perhaps from a # re-consent that was appended rather than replaced demo_dup <- tibble(patient_id = c("P001", "P001", "P002"), age = c(64, 65, 71)) vis <- tibble(patient_id = c("P001", "P002"), sbp = c(148, 155)) # the silent version: two rows become three left_join(vis, demo_dup, by = "patient_id") #> # A tibble: 3 x 3 #> patient_id sbp age #> #> 1 P001 148 64 #> 2 P001 148 65 #> 3 P002 155 71 # the assertion, before anything downstream runs stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(demo_dup$patient_id)) #> Error: #> ! !anyDuplicated(demo_dup$patient_id) is not TRUE ``` ::: The join itself does not fail. It quietly returns more rows than it received, and because `vis` has unique keys, `dplyr` does not even warn. The `stopifnot()` fails loudly, which is the behavior you want. Declaring `relationship = "many-to-one"` on the join achieves the same thing at the point of use. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** You join `visits` (10,000 rows) to `demographics` (1,000 patients) on `patient_id`. The result has 12,500 rows. What likely happened, and how do you find out? **Answer.** The demographics table has duplicate `patient_id` values, and each duplicate creates extra rows in the join output. A clean many-to-one join returns 10,000 rows, one per visit. The 2,500 extra rows are the visits of patients with more than one demographics record. Diagnose with: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} demographics |> count(patient_id) |> filter(n > 1) #> # A tibble: 0 x 2 #> # i 2 variables: patient_id , n ``` ::: Fix the duplication at its source. The tempting shortcut is `distinct(patient_id, .keep_all = TRUE)`. It keeps whichever row for each patient happens to come first. That is, it chooses a record by file order rather than by any rule. If the duplicates disagree on age or sex, which one survives is an accident. If de-duplication is right, state the rule in code (the most recent record, say, with `slice_max()` on a date column). Adding `relationship = "many-to-one"` to the join catches the problem at the join site. ::: ## Keys and referential integrity {#sec-joins-keys} A join that returns the number of rows you predicted usually did what you meant. A join that returns 'about the right number' is where the bugs are usually found. The checks below run before the analytic join and take seconds. ### Auditing keys before the join Two CRF (case report form) files that should cover the same patients usually do not match exactly. `anti_join()` lists the patients on one side that are absent from the other. It is the quickest way to find missing records, ID typos, or a cohort mismatch. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # uniqueness of keys demographics |> distinct(patient_id) |> nrow() #> [1] 3 demographics |> nrow() #> [1] 3 # These should match for one-row-per-patient # stopifnot for assertion stopifnot(!any(duplicated(demographics$patient_id))) # anti-join audit visits |> anti_join(demographics, by = "patient_id") |> distinct(patient_id) #> # A tibble: 1 x 1 #> patient_id #> #> 1 P004 # patients in visits with no demographics row ``` ::: `assertthat` and `assertr` provide more elaborate assertions. For most work, `stopifnot()` plus `anti_join()` audits cover the cases. ### Composite keys When no single column identifies a row, name every column of the key: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} reference_ranges <- tibble( test_code = c("HGB", "HGB", "CRE"), sex = c("F", "M", "F"), age_group = c("50-70", "50-70", "50-70"), lower = c(12.0, 13.5, 0.6), upper = c(15.5, 17.5, 1.1) ) labs |> left_join(visits, by = "visit_id") |> left_join(demographics, by = "patient_id") |> mutate(age_group = "50-70") |> left_join(reference_ranges, by = c("test_code", "sex", "age_group")) #> # A tibble: 4 x 10 #> visit_id test_code value patient_id sbp age sex age_group lower upper #> #> 1 V01 HGB 13.1 P001 148 64 F 50-70 12 15.5 #> 2 V01 CRE 0.9 P001 148 64 F 50-70 0.6 1.1 #> 3 V02 HGB 13.4 P001 141 64 F 50-70 12 15.5 #> 4 V03 HGB 11.8 P002 155 71 M 50-70 13.5 17.5 ``` ::: ### Key types and representation Document the canonical form of every identifier (character, with leading zeros, upper case) and check it on every read. `dplyr` refuses to join a character key to a numeric one. That failure is easy to see. The failure that is hard to see is two character keys that spell the same patient differently. ::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'} **Lost leading zeros match nothing, and the row count does not move.** If one file was read with `patient_id` as a number and later converted with `as.character()`, `"001"` has become `"1"`. A `left_join` on that key returns every row of the left table, which is the count you expected. However, every right-hand column is `NA`. Read identifiers as character from the start (`col_types = cols(patient_id = col_character())`). ::: ### Aside: updating a table by key with `rows_*` The `rows_*` verbs update one table from another by key, and they enforce key integrity as they go. They suit updating a master patient list from a new extract. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} target <- tibble(id = 1:3, value = c("a", "b", NA)) source <- tibble(id = 3:4, value = c("c", "d")) # insert new rows; error on key collision rows_insert(target, source, by = "id") #> Error in `rows_insert()`: #> ! `y` can't contain keys that already exist in `x`. #> i The following rows in `y` have keys that already exist in `x`: `c(1)`. #> i Use `conflict = "ignore"` if you want to ignore these `y` rows. # update existing rows; error if key not in target rows_update(target, source, by = "id") #> Error in `rows_update()`: #> ! `y` must contain keys that already exist in `x`. #> i The following rows in `y` have keys that don't exist in `x`: `c(2)`. #> i Use `unmatched = "ignore"` if you want to ignore these `y` rows. # upsert: insert new, update existing rows_upsert(target, source, by = "id") #> # A tibble: 4 x 2 #> id value #> #> 1 1 a #> 2 2 b #> 3 3 c #> 4 4 d # patch: only update where target has NA; id 4 is not in target, # so it must be ignored explicitly rows_patch(target, source, by = "id", unmatched = "ignore") #> # A tibble: 3 x 2 #> id value #> #> 1 1 a #> 2 2 b #> 3 3 c ``` ::: `rows_upsert` adds new patients and updates existing ones. `rows_patch` fills in missing values without overwriting existing ones. ### Exercises 3. Use `rows_upsert` to merge two cohorts with overlapping patients (some new, some updated). Verify the result has the expected number of rows. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} cohort_1 <- tibble(patient_id = c("P001", "P002"), status = c("enrolled", "enrolled")) cohort_2 <- tibble(patient_id = c("P002", "P003"), status = c("withdrawn", "enrolled")) merged <- rows_upsert(cohort_1, cohort_2, by = "patient_id") merged #> # A tibble: 3 x 2 #> patient_id status #> #> 1 P001 enrolled #> 2 P002 withdrawn #> 3 P003 enrolled # two originals plus one genuinely new patient stopifnot(nrow(merged) == 3) ``` ::: P002 is updated in place rather than duplicated, and P003 is inserted. The row count distinguishes an upsert from an accidental `bind_rows()`. The latter would have produced four rows and two conflicting records for P002. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** You `left_join` a 500-row visits table to a demographics table and get 500 rows back, which is what you expected. A colleague says this proves nothing. Are they right? **Answer.** They are. A row count matching your expectation rules out duplication and rules out nothing else. Every `patient_id` in visits could have failed to match, and `left_join` would still return exactly 500 rows, each with `NA` in every demographics column. The lost-leading-zeros case above does exactly this. The count does not catch this, but two other checks do. First, count the `NA`s in a column that came from the right-hand table. The count should be zero if every visit has demographics. Second, run the anti-join: ```r visits |> anti_join(demographics, by = "patient_id") |> distinct(patient_id) ``` An empty result means every key matched. A result listing every patient means the join silently did nothing. `nrow()` is a structural check, in the sense @sec-testing gives that term, and structural checks can pass on wrong answers. ::: ## Reshaping and stacking sources {#sec-joins-reshaping} Some joins need wide data and others need long data. @sec-wrangling covers `pivot_longer()` and `pivot_wider()`. When several sources hold alternative measurements of the same kind, the usual pattern is: 1. Convert each source to long format with consistent column names. 2. Stack the sources with `bind_rows()` rather than joining them. 3. Pivot wide for the modeling step. For two CRF files from sites A and B with different column conventions (display-only; the files are hypothetical): ```r a_long <- read_csv("siteA.csv") |> clean_names() |> rename(bp_systolic = systolic_bp) |> pivot_longer(starts_with("bp_"), names_to = "measure") b_long <- read_csv("siteB.csv") |> clean_names() |> pivot_longer(matches("^(bp|sbp|dbp)_"), names_to = "measure") combined <- bind_rows(a_long, b_long) ``` `bind_rows()` stacks tables. `bind_cols()` places tables side by side by position. That is rarely correct for clinical data, because nothing checks that row 12 of one table is the same patient as row 12 of the other. When the tables share a key, join on it. ### Exercises 4. Two wide tables represent patient visits at sites A and B with different column-name conventions. Reshape both to long and stack them so that downstream analysis treats them uniformly. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyr) site_a <- tibble(patient_id = "A01", systolic_bp = 148, diastolic_bp = 88) site_b <- tibble(patient_id = "B01", sbp_1 = 155, dbp_1 = 91) a_long <- site_a |> rename(bp_systolic = systolic_bp, bp_diastolic = diastolic_bp) |> pivot_longer(starts_with("bp_"), names_to = "measure") b_long <- site_b |> rename(bp_systolic = sbp_1, bp_diastolic = dbp_1) |> pivot_longer(starts_with("bp_"), names_to = "measure") bind_rows(a_long, b_long, .id = "site") #> # A tibble: 4 x 4 #> site patient_id measure value #> #> 1 1 A01 bp_systolic 148 #> 2 1 A01 bp_diastolic 88 #> 3 2 B01 bp_systolic 155 #> 4 2 B01 bp_diastolic 91 ``` ::: Renaming to a shared vocabulary *before* the pivot is what makes `bind_rows()` safe. Stacking first and reconciling after leaves you matching on strings that do not agree. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** The long `labs` table has one row per visit and test. You join it directly to `visits` on `visit_id`. What relationship is that, and what happens to a later model that expects one row per visit? **Answer.** One-to-many: a visit with two tests appears twice. Any per-visit model then counts that visit twice. Pivot `labs` wide first, to one row per visit, and declare `relationship = "one-to-one"` on the join. The worked example below does both. ::: ## Worked example: a multi-source patient cohort {#sec-joins-worked} The script below runs against the three fixture tables shown earlier. They are written out as files, so that the script reads them as it would read a real export. P004, who has visits but no demographics row, is planted deliberately, so the audit warns once. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) #> -- Attaching core tidyverse packages ------------------------ tidyverse 2.0.0 -- #> v forcats 1.0.1 v readr 2.2.0 #> v ggplot2 4.0.3 v stringr 1.6.0 #> v lubridate 1.9.5 v tibble 3.3.1 #> v purrr 1.2.2 #> -- Conflicts ------------------------------------------ tidyverse_conflicts() -- #> x dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter() #> x dplyr::lag() masks stats::lag() #> i Use the conflicted package () to force all conflicts to become errors library(janitor) #> #> Attaching package: 'janitor' #> #> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats': #> #> chisq.test, fisher.test src <- file.path(tempdir(), "cohort") dir.create(src, showWarnings = FALSE) write_csv(demographics, file.path(src, "demographics.csv")) write_csv(visits, file.path(src, "visits.csv")) write_csv(labs, file.path(src, "labs.csv")) # read three sources demographics <- read_csv(file.path(src, "demographics.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |> clean_names() visits <- read_csv(file.path(src, "visits.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |> clean_names() labs <- read_csv(file.path(src, "labs.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |> clean_names() # labs is long, one row per visit and test, so its key is the pair stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(demographics$patient_id)) stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(visits$visit_id)) stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(labs[c("visit_id", "test_code")])) # audit: patients in visits but no demographics missing_demo <- visits |> anti_join(demographics, by = "patient_id") |> distinct(patient_id) if (nrow(missing_demo) > 0) { warning("Patients in visits with no demographics: ", paste(missing_demo$patient_id, collapse = ", ")) } #> Warning: Patients in visits with no demographics: P004 # one row per visit, so that the lab join cannot add rows labs_wide <- labs |> pivot_wider(names_from = test_code, values_from = value) |> clean_names() # build the analytic dataset analytic <- visits |> left_join(demographics, by = "patient_id", relationship = "many-to-one", unmatched = "error") |> left_join(labs_wide, by = "visit_id", relationship = "one-to-one") |> mutate( age_group = cut(age, breaks = c(0, 40, 65, Inf)) ) # final row-count check: neither join may add or drop visits stopifnot(nrow(analytic) == nrow(visits)) saveRDS(analytic, file.path(src, "analytic.rds")) analytic #> # A tibble: 6 x 8 #> visit_id patient_id sbp age sex hgb cre age_group #> #> 1 V01 P001 148 64 F 13.1 0.9 (40,65] #> 2 V02 P001 141 64 F 13.4 NA (40,65] #> 3 V03 P002 155 71 M 11.8 NA (65,Inf] #> 4 V04 P002 149 71 M NA NA (65,Inf] #> 5 V05 P003 132 52 F NA NA (40,65] #> 6 V06 P004 139 NA NA NA ``` ::: The script cleans names and verifies key uniqueness, using the composite key for the long `labs` table. It runs an `anti_join()` audit and reshapes `labs` to one row per visit. It then performs the joins with explicit `relationship` declarations, and asserts the final row count. Joining the long `labs` table directly would have been one-to-many. It would have returned seven rows from six visits and failed the final check. A reviewer can read the script and trust the join semantics without re-deriving them. `unmatched = "error"` is the companion to `relationship`. `relationship` constrains how many rows each key matches. `unmatched` constrains whether keys go unmatched at all. For a left join it checks only the right-hand table. Here, therefore, it stops the script if a patient in `demographics` has no visits. The `anti_join()` audit covers the other direction. ::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'} Confirm that the analytic dataset has one row per visit and that the only visits without demographics are the ones the audit named. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} stopifnot( nrow(analytic) == nrow(visits), !anyDuplicated(analytic$visit_id) ) analytic |> filter(is.na(age)) |> distinct(patient_id) #> # A tibble: 1 x 1 #> patient_id #> #> 1 P004 ``` ::: The second line should list P004 and nobody else. Any other patient here is a key that failed to match without an error. ::: ### The join checklist Every join in the worked example passes the same seven checks, collected in @tbl-join-checklist. They apply unchanged to joins written in SQL (@sec-databases) and to the analysis datasets an analysis plan specifies (@sec-analysis-plan). | When | Check | Code | |---|---|---| | Before | The key is unique on the side that should have one row per key | `stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(x$key))` | | Before | Key types and spelling agree (character, leading zeros, case) | `class(x$key)`; `head(sort(unique(x$key)))` | | Before | Coverage in each direction | `anti_join(x, y, by = "key")` and `anti_join(y, x, by = "key")` | | During | The relationship is declared | `relationship = "many-to-one"` | | During | Unmatched keys are refused where none are allowed | `unmatched = "error"` | | After | The row count is the one you predicted | `stopifnot(nrow(out) == nrow(x))` | | After | Right-hand columns are not unexpectedly `NA` | `sum(is.na(out$col_from_y))` | : The join checklist. Run it on every non-trivial join; the first three rows take seconds and catch most join bugs before they happen. {#tbl-join-checklist} ::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'} In an agentic version, a coding agent adds the assertions and runs the script. You then review the evidence it reports, not only its code. > **Context.** `R/build_analytic.R` joins `visits` (key > `visit_id`; `patient_id` repeats) to `demographics` (one row per > `patient_id`) and to `labs` (one row per `visit_id` and > `test_code`). Column names and types are in > `data/dictionary.csv`. Run the script only against the synthetic > fixtures in `tests/fixtures/`. > > **Constraints.** Use `dplyr`. Add `relationship =` to every join, > and `unmatched = "error"` wherever no key should go unmatched. > Add a `stopifnot()` row-count check after each join. Do not > change a join type, add `distinct()` or `filter()`, or declare > `"many-to-many"` to make a check pass. Add no packages. > > **Criteria.** Before writing code, state the relationship you > expect for each join and list your assumptions. After running, > report for each join the row counts before and after and the > anti-join audit in both directions. If any check fails, stop and > report it instead of fixing it. *Failure mode.* The agent silences a failing check by declaring `"many-to-many"` or inserting `distinct()`. Either change hides the duplicate that the check found. *Check.* Search the diff for `many-to-many`, `distinct(`, and new `filter(` calls. Then run the script yourself and go through @tbl-join-checklist. The agent sees the dictionary, code, and synthetic rows, never patient data (@sec-ai-governance). ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** In the worked example, why does the script pivot `labs` wide *before* the join instead of after it? **Answer.** Because the join to `visits` is meant to be one-to-one. Pivoting first makes `visit_id` unique in `labs_wide`, so `relationship = "one-to-one"` can be declared and the final `nrow(analytic) == nrow(visits)` check can hold. Joining the long table and pivoting afterward would multiply the visit rows in the intermediate result. Any summary computed on that intermediate would silently count some visits twice. ::: ## Rules of thumb 1. **Habit 6: count before and after every join.** Predict the row count, declare `relationship =` and, where it applies, `unmatched = "error"`, and let the code refuse anything else. 2. **Habit 8: a join that drops or multiplies rows produces a plausible number.** A matching row count is a structural check. Pair it with an anti-join audit and an `NA` count on the right-hand columns. 3. **Habit 7: convert late, validate early.** Read identifiers as character, document their canonical form, and check it before the first join. ## Cumulative practice 5. *Cumulative (uses @sec-git-teams).* Review a colleague's multi-table script (or one from a public analysis repository) for join safety alone. For every join, determine the intended relationship, check whether a `relationship` argument asserts it, and run an `anti_join()` audit on the keys. Report what you find as you would in a pull-request comment, naming the specific line and the specific risk, and use @tbl-join-checklist as your rubric. 6. *On your own work (no key).* Take a recent multi-table analysis of yours. Audit each join with `anti_join()` to identify missing keys, and document any unexpected gaps. ## Cheat sheet | Task | Code | Guards against | |---|---|---| | Keep matched rows only | `inner_join(x, y, by = "id")` | Unmatched rows (by dropping them) | | Keep every row of `x` | `left_join(x, y, by = "id")` | Losing cohort members | | Find rows of `x` with no match | `anti_join(x, y, by = "id")` | Silent gaps between files | | Keep rows of `x` that match | `semi_join(x, y, by = "id")` | Adding columns you do not need | | Assert the relationship | `relationship = "many-to-one"` | Row multiplication | | Refuse unmatched `y` keys | `unmatched = "error"` | Silent non-matches | | Find duplicated keys | `filter(count(x, id), n > 1)` | Duplicates before they join | | Assert the row count | `stopifnot(nrow(out) == nrow(x))` | Rows added or dropped | | Join on several columns | `by = c("test_code", "sex")` | Matching on a partial key | | Update a table by key | `rows_upsert(x, y, by = "id")` | Duplicate records on update | | Stack like sources | `bind_rows(a, b, .id = "site")` | Joining what should be stacked | : Joins at a glance. {#tbl-joins-cheat-sheet} ## Further reading - [@wickham2023r4ds] Chapters 19 and 20, the `dplyr` two-table verbs. - [@bryan2019stat545] Chapters 14 to 16, joins and lookups. - The `dplyr` 1.1.0 release notes for the `relationship` argument and the many-to-many warning. ## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-15} 1. `inner_join()` returns only rows whose key matches in both tables. `left_join()` returns every row from the left table; rows with no match on the right get `NA` in the right-hand columns. If the left table has 100 rows with keys A to J and the right table has only keys A to F, `inner_join` returns 60 rows and `left_join` returns 100 rows (40 with `NA`s). 2. `anti_join(x, y)` returns rows of `x` whose key is *not* present in `y`. In a biomedical cleanup workflow it answers: 'Which patients appear in my outcome file but not in the lab data?' (or the reverse). It thereby exposes missing records, miscoded IDs, or mismatched cohorts. It does not detect duplicate IDs, which need a `count()` on the key. Run it before the analytic join, so that problems surface early. 3. `table_a |> left_join(table_b, by = 'patient_id', relationship = 'many-to-one')`. A many-to-one join attaches the single table-B row to every table-A row sharing the key. The `relationship` argument errors if the relationship does not hold (for example, if `patient_id` is duplicated in table B).
